name: Grants
title: Grants
answer: Grants can bring significant resources to schools, but finding them and writing applications takes staff time. AI can help staff search federal and state grant listings and draft parts of applications, while people verify every fact, figure, and claim. This matters because false information in an application can cost funding, and grant compliance tracking helps districts meet the conditions of the money they receive.

sections.body: This idea is about using AI as a support tool for grant work, not as an authority. Staff can use it to locate possible grants from federal and state listings and to produce early drafts of application sections. The problem it solves is the time burden of grant writing and the difficulty of keeping track of funding opportunities. It also addresses compliance, because districts must meet conditions attached to funding and report on spending and deadlines. The text frames AI as a helper for search and drafting, with people responsible for accuracy and review.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district office, staff can ask AI tools to search federal and state grant listings and to draft sections of applications. Spreadsheet tools with AI can help track spending, deadlines, and reporting requirements for grants the district has received. The grant manager reviews the tracking and confirms that reports are accurate. The text does not give grade bands for this practice, so it applies to the central staff and grant managers who handle funding rather than to a particular classroom level. Teachers and school leaders may supply information about needs or programs, but the application and compliance work sits with the grant team.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It says only that AI tools can invent statistics, citations, and details that sound real, and it refers back to Chapter 1, which described how these tools produce confident errors. It also states that a made up statistic about student needs or program results could be treated as a false statement in a grant application. On that basis, the idea rests on practice and on the book's earlier account of AI error, not on a cited research finding.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Every fact, figure, and claim in a grant application must be verified by a person. Staff should check each number against the district's own data and each citation against its source. The grant manager reviews compliance tracking and makes sure reports are accurate. The text warns that false information can lead to lost funding or worse, and that compliance failures can require districts to return money. The decisions about what to submit, what the data show, and whether a report is accurate stay with people, not with the AI tool.
